newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN experts find 80 bodies in Vukovar mass grave.
newsitem.headline: UN experts find 80 bodies in Vukovar mass grave.

text.p: International investigators have uncovered 80 bodies in a grave site near Vukovar, believed to contain remains of hospital patients executed after Serb forces seized the town in 1991, Croatian media reported on Wednesday.
Some 60 bodies from Vukovar were transferred this week to Zagreb for autopsy, the state news agency Hina reported, quoting the head of the U.N. forensic team William Haglund.

Haglund, who carries out excavations of mass grave sites in former Yugoslavia on behalf of the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague, said that "at least 40" more bodies were visible in the pit at Ovcara near Vukovar.
"The process could be finished in the next five days, though it could take more or even less," Haglund told a news conference in Vukovar in Eastern Slavonia.
He said the exact number of bodies would not be known before the grave site was completely excavated. The autopsy could begin by the middle of next week, and would last for four to eight weeks.
International and local media are banned from the site, located in the last Serb-held enclave of Eastern Slavonia, to avoid stirring up emotions that could harm the peace process, U.N. officials say.
The area, controlled by U.N. peacekeepers, is scheduled to come under Zagreb government control by the end of 1997 at the latest.
Haglund said only bodies of men have been found so far, and some bore traces of suffering trauma injuries.
Certain objects indicating that the victims were hospital patients, such as plaster casts, have also been found beside the bodies, Haglund said.

Circumstantial evidence and eyewitness accounts suggest that Yugoslav army and Serb irregulars executed around 200 Croats, patients of the Vukovar hospital, in the days following their capture of the town in November 1991, war crimes prosecutors say.
The Hague tribunal indicted three Yugoslav army officers for war crimes and crimes against humanity for the Ovcara killings.
Vukovar fell to Serb forces after a three-month siege combined with artillery bombardments that reduced it to rubble.
Croatia declared independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia earlier that year, sparking a Serb insurgence supported by the federal army and Serbian volunteers.
